transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi Doctor. I just... I really didn't know where else to go, because things have gotten so strange lately and it's really wearing me down. I work as a personal care aide, you know, and it’s a hard job, you're on your feet all day, you're lifting people, making sure they're okay, so when I finally get off my shift and go home to my little studio apartment, I just want some peace. 

But I came in because... well, I keep hearing these voices. And it’s not like the TV being left on next door or muffled sounds through the wall, I mean it is as clear as somebody standing right there in the middle of my little studio with me. They keep saying my name, just clear as day, and telling me that my work is being judged. And I don't know why they'd say that because I work so hard for my clients and I do my best, but it just keeps happening and it's so stressful. 

And the scariest part is, the house is completely quiet. I live alone. I check the deadbolt, I check the bathroom, I look in the closet, and nobody is there. Not a single soul. But I still hear them, just as loud and clear as you and me talking right now, judging everything I do when there is absolutely nobody else in the room. I just... I can't take it anymore, it's making me so upset because I just want to sit in my quiet apartment and rest, but they won't stop talking to me.
Can you tell me exactly when these voices first started—how many days, weeks, or months ago?

Well, let me think back... if I have to put an exact timeline on it, it’s been going on for a long time now. I’d say it’s been right about nine months. Yes, nine whole months of this absolute nightmare. 

I remember it clearly because it was right around the time I started picking up extra shifts for a new client, and I’d come home just dead tired, my feet swollen and my back aching like you wouldn't believe from all the lifting and transferring. I sat down on my little floral sofa—the one I got second-hand over on Elm Street, it's very comfortable but it's getting a bit worn out—and I heard it for the very first time. I thought someone had followed me inside! And ever since that evening, for nine solid months, it just hasn't stopped. 

And it’s not just the talking, it’s this... this terrible, heavy fear that’s settled right in my chest that they are actually watching everything I do at my job. That someone is monitoring me and grading me every time I adjust a bedpan or help someone out of a wheelchair or even just pour them a glass of water. Nine months of looking over my shoulder, double-checking my work, coming home and checking the locks because I'm so scared someone is keeping tabs on me. I mean, you try doing physical labor all day and then coming home to that for nine months straight... it just wears a person down to the bone, it really does. I just want it to be quiet again like it was last year.
During these nine months, have you been using any alcohol, recreational drugs, or other substances regularly?

Oh, goodness, no. No, no, no. I don't even have the time or the money for anything like that, let alone the energy. When you're a personal care aide, you have to be sharp, you know? You literally have people's safety in your hands. If I'm transferring one of my heavier clients—like this one lady I see on Tuesdays and Thursdays, bless her heart, she's completely bedbound—if I'm moving her and I've got a hangover or I'm on some kind of pill, I could drop her. I could really hurt her. And I would never, ever forgive myself for something like that. 

I don't even drink a glass of wine on the holidays. My sister, she likes her margaritas on the weekends, and she's always saying, "Oh, come on, just have one, it'll help you relax," especially lately since I've been so high-strung and exhausted with the voices and the feeling of being watched all the time. But I tell her, absolutely not, I need a clear head. I just drink my regular drip coffee in the morning, maybe two cups if it's a double shift, and that is it. No drugs, no alcohol, no nothing. 

I wouldn't even know where to buy recreational drugs if I wanted to, which I certainly don't! I'm fifty-five years old. I just go to work, do my job, come home to my apartment, and lock the deadbolt. That's my whole entire life right there. So no, definitely no substances. I just don't understand why my mind is playing these terrible tricks on me when I live such a clean, quiet life, you know? I try to do everything right.

Over these past nine months, have you also noticed periods where your mood was very low—like feeling deeply depressed or hopeless—or on the other hand, unusually elevated, energetic, or 'high,' alongside the voices?

Well, yes, actually. Yes, I have. It's funny you mention the energetic part, because... well, a few months ago—maybe around month four or five of all this—I had this spell where I just felt incredible. I mean, I was practically buzzing. I didn't even need to sleep. I'd come home from a double shift, completely wired, and maybe I'd lay down for two, maybe three hours tops, and then I'd pop right back up, feeling like I could conquer the world. 

And I had these ideas, these huge, grand ideas. I decided I was going to revolutionize personal care by integrating art therapy. I went out and spent money I didn't really have on all these paints and canvases and clay, just filling up my little studio apartment with it. I was staying up all night drafting these elaborate business plans, writing these long, passionate letters to the local nursing homes about how my "art-and-care" program was going to change everything. I felt so brilliant, so unstoppable, like I had finally cracked the code to happiness for all these elderly folks. 

But the thing is... the whole time I was doing that, the whole time I was running on no sleep and pushing these massive plans, the voices were still there. I'd be sitting on my worn-out floral sofa at 3:00 AM, painting furiously, and I'd hear them right over my shoulder, clear as day, telling me my work was being judged. I still felt that heavy, terrifying certainty that people were watching me, monitoring my every brushstroke, grading my plans. So even when I felt like I was on top of the world, I was still terrified in my own home. 

And then, of course, the energy just... crashed. It just evaporated. After a few weeks of that, I woke up one morning and I couldn't even get out of bed. I felt so heavy, so incredibly sad and hopeless. I looked around at all the art supplies and just cried because it all seemed so stupid and pointless. I dragged myself to work, but it was like moving through molasses. I felt so worthless, like I was the worst personal care aide in the world, and I just wanted to disappear. And through all of that dark, heavy depression, the voices never stopped. They just kept right on talking, right on judging me, no matter if I was flying high or sinking low. It’s just been a constant, exhausting companion through all these ups and downs.

Outside of that manic period and the depressive crash, during the other months when your mood was more your usual baseline, did you still hear the voices and feel that you were being watched and judged?

Yes, yes, they absolutely did. It's the strangest thing, and honestly, it's the most frustrating part of all of this. Because you see, after that terrible, heavy crash where I could barely move and just cried over all those expensive art supplies... eventually, that dark cloud sort of lifted. My energy went back to just my regular, everyday level—not that crazy buzzing feeling where I didn't need to sleep, and not that awful heaviness either. 

I actually started sleeping normally again. Just my regular old schedule, you know? Going to bed at ten, locking the deadbolt, waking up at five-thirty for my shifts, getting a solid night's rest just like I used to before all this started. And I remember thinking, well, maybe now that I'm feeling more like plain old me again, maybe my brain will finally quiet down. I really, really hoped it would. I thought, okay, the sadness is gone, the wild energy is gone, so surely the voices will pack up and leave too.

But they didn't. Not at all. There was this whole stretch of time right after my energy leveled out and my sleep went back to normal... it went on for several weeks, just day in and day out. My mood was perfectly fine, just my usual baseline, just going to work and coming home, but those voices were still right there in my ear. And that awful, heavy belief that people were tracking my work and grading my every move... that kept going for several weeks too, completely unchanged. 

I'd be at my client's house, feeling totally fine emotionally, just doing my normal routine, maybe fixing them a plate of scrambled eggs or helping them put their compression socks on—which is a real chore, let me tell you, those socks are so tight—and I'd still hear the whispering. I'd still feel those eyes on the back of my neck, judging me, making sure I wasn't messing up. It just didn't matter that I wasn't high as a kite or low as dirt anymore. For weeks and weeks of just being my normal self, the nightmare just kept right on playing. It makes you feel like you can't ever truly escape it, no matter how normal your mood is, you know? Because even when I was fine, they were still there.

Adding up all the time since this started nine months ago, would you say the manic or depressed periods together lasted for more than half of that time, or was most of the nine months spent with your mood at that normal baseline while the voices continued?

Well, if I really sit down and try to add it all up... let me think about that. Because time gets so funny, you know? When you're working these long shifts and your brain is just constantly going, the days just sort of bleed into one another. But... but if I'm being completely honest, looking back over the whole nine months since this nightmare started? I'd have to say the normal parts were really just a drop in the bucket compared to the rest of it. 

For most of this stretch, I was either completely wound up with those big plans I told you about, getting practically no sleep and just running on nonstop activity, or... or I was coming down from all that and crashing hard, but still just not back to myself at all. It felt like the rollercoaster just went on and on. I mean, that period where I was buying all the paint and staying up all night writing those letters to the nursing homes, that alone dragged on for a good long while, and then the awful, heavy sadness that came after it seemed to last forever too. 

So, yes, even though I did have those few weeks of just being plain old me with my regular sleep schedule—which I was so grateful for, even with the whispering still going on—if you look at the whole calendar, most of the nine months was definitely taken up by either flying too high or sinking too low. It was just month after month of either being totally wired and unstoppable or feeling like I couldn't even drag myself out of bed to go care for my ladies. The normal days were definitely the exception, not the rule, which just breaks my heart because I just want to be back to my regular life all the time.

Well, if I really sit down and try to add it all up... let me think about that. Because time gets so funny, you know? When you're working these long shifts and your brain is just constantly going, the days just sort of bleed into one another. But... but if I'm being completely honest, looking back over the whole nine months since this nightmare started? I'd have to say the normal parts were really just a drop in the bucket compared to the rest of it. 

For most of this stretch, I was either completely wound up with those big plans I told you about, getting practically no sleep and just running on nonstop activity, or... or I was coming down from all that and crashing hard, but still just not back to myself at all. It felt like the rollercoaster just went on and on. I mean, that period where I was buying all the paint and staying up all night writing those letters to the nursing homes, that alone dragged on for a good long while, and then the awful, heavy sadness that came after it seemed to last forever too. 

So, yes, even though I did have those few weeks of just being plain old me with my regular sleep schedule—which I was so grateful for, even with the whispering still going on—if you look at the whole calendar, most of the nine months was definitely taken up by either flying too high or sinking too low. It was just month after month of either being totally wired and unstoppable or feeling like I couldn't even drag myself out of bed to go care for my ladies. The normal days were definitely the exception, not the rule, which just breaks my heart because I just want to be back to my regular life all the time.

inference.note: Patient confirms manic and depressive episodes together occupied the majority of the 9-month illness duration, with psychotic symptoms persisting even during a normal-mood interval, meeting schizoaffective disorder criteria. Presence of a manic episode (not just depressive) supports bipolar type over depressive type, ruling out F25.1.
